text: The statement provisions distinguish a relevant oral statement made in known-agent interrogation that the government intends to use at trial from the broader specified written, recorded, recorded-oral, and grand-jury statements covered by Rule 16(a)(1)(B). [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)(A)–(B)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Each statement category has distinct interrogation, intent-to-use, possession, and knowledge conditions.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: On request and subject to the rule's possession, knowledge, materiality, intended-use, and ownership conditions, Rule 16(a)(1) also covers the defendant's prior record, documents and objects, examination and test reports, and expert-witness information. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)(D)–(G)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The request and each category's rule-text conditions must be proved.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For Rule 16 expert disclosures, the court by order or local rule must set a time sufficiently before trial to give the opposing side a fair opportunity to meet the evidence, and the current rule specifies the required opinions, bases, reasons, qualifications, prior publications, prior testimony, approval, signature, and supplementation information. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)(G), (b)(1)(C)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The controlling court order or local rule supplies the actual disclosure date.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 16(a)(2) ordinarily excludes internal government reports and memoranda and does not authorize discovery of prospective government-witness statements except as 18 U.S.C. § 3500 provides; Rule 16(a)(3) separately limits discovery of recorded grand-jury proceedings. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(2)–(3)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3500](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Independent constitutional and Rule 26.2 duties are not decided by the Rule 16 exclusion.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The defendant's reciprocal document, report, and expert duties arise only under the conditions stated in Rule 16(b), including a qualifying defense request followed by government compliance or the expert-disclosure request specified in the rule. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(b)(1)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The actual request, government compliance, intended use, and possession control.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 16(c) imposes a continuing duty to disclose newly discovered evidence or material before or during trial when it is subject to Rule 16 and the opposing party previously requested, or the court ordered, production. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(c)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The item must remain within Rule 16 and have been requested or ordered.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For good cause, Rule 16(d)(1) permits a court to deny, restrict, or defer discovery, or grant other appropriate relief, including on an ex parte written showing whose complete text the court must preserve under seal if relief is granted. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(d)(1)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Privileges, classified information, victim protection, and local sealing law require separate authority.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For a Rule 16 violation, the court may order discovery on just terms, grant a continuance, prohibit use of undisclosed evidence, or enter another order just under the circumstances; the rule does not make one sanction automatic for every violation. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(d)(2)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Appellate standards and case-specific sanction selection require controlling circuit law.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: No later than 14 days after arraignment, Rule 16.1(a) requires government and defense counsel to confer and try to agree on a timetable and procedures for Rule 16 disclosure; after that conference, either or both may ask the court to determine or modify disclosure arrangements. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16.1](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The actual arraignment date, computation, extensions, and court orders control.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 45(a) supplies federal criminal time computation, and Rule 45(b)(1) permits extension before expiration for good cause or after expiration for excusable neglect; Rule 16.1 is not among Rule 45(b)(2)'s listed no-extension provisions. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 45(a)–(b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: No jurisdictional characterization is made; an actual extension requires the rule's showing and an order.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 16, the Jencks Act, and the *Brady* line are separate sources with different triggers and coverage, so an item may require independent classification under more than one source rather than treatment under a single generic “discovery” rule. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3500](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500); [*Brady v. Maryland*, 373 U.S. 83, 86–88 (1963)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-373/pdf/USREPORTS-373-83.pdf)
known_limitations: Overlap does not erase any source's distinct trigger, scope, or remedy.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: A true *Brady* violation has three components: evidence favorable to the accused, suppression by the government willfully or inadvertently, and resulting prejudice. [*Strickler v. Greene*, 527 U.S. 263, 281–82 (1999)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-527/pdf/USREPORTS-527-263.pdf); [*Brady*, 373 U.S. at 87](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-373/pdf/USREPORTS-373-83.pdf)
known_limitations: Application requires the complete record and the allegedly suppressed evidence.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Evidence may be favorable because it is exculpatory or because it impeaches a prosecution witness; impeachment evidence is not categorically outside the constitutional disclosure rule. [*Strickler*, 527 U.S. at 281–82](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-527/pdf/USREPORTS-527-263.pdf); [*United States v. Bagley*, 473 U.S. 667, 676–78 (1985)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf)
known_limitations: Favorability and materiality remain case-specific.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The constitutional disclosure duty is not eliminated by the absence of a specific defense request: *Bagley* applies its materiality formulation to no-request, general-request, and specific-request nondisclosure. [*Bagley*, 473 U.S. at 682–83](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf)
known_limitations: A request may still matter to suppression, notice, remedies, and local procedure.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The prosecution's good faith does not defeat a *Brady* claim, because suppression may be willful or inadvertent; prejudice and the other constitutional components remain required. [*Brady*, 373 U.S. at 87](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-373/pdf/USREPORTS-373-83.pdf); [*Strickler*, 527 U.S. at 281–82](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-527/pdf/USREPORTS-527-263.pdf)
known_limitations: Good faith does not eliminate the claim, but favorability, suppression, and prejudice remain required.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Suppressed favorable evidence is material under *Bagley* when there is a reasonable probability that disclosure would have produced a different result, meaning a probability sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome. [*Bagley*, 473 U.S. at 682](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf)
known_limitations: The standard must be applied to the complete case and requested remedy.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: *Kyles* requires materiality to be assessed collectively, not item by item, and makes clear that the inquiry is not a sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence test or a constitutional open-file mandate. [*Kyles v. Whitley*, 514 U.S. 419, 434–37 (1995)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-514/pdf/USREPORTS-514-419.pdf)
known_limitations: The prosecution's broader ethical or policy duties are not equated with the constitutional minimum.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The individual prosecutor must learn of favorable evidence known to others acting on the government's behalf in the case, including police, but determining who falls within that case-specific group requires the actual investigative relationships and controlling law. [*Kyles*, 514 U.S. at 437–38](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-514/pdf/USREPORTS-514-419.pdf)
known_limitations: Case-specific team boundaries require investigative facts and controlling circuit law.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: *Giglio* treats an undisclosed promise of nonprosecution to a key government witness as credibility evidence within the due-process rule when the witness's reliability may determine guilt or innocence; it does not require a new trial for every item that might have been useful to the defense. [*Giglio v. United States*, 405 U.S. 150, 153–55 (1972)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-405/pdf/USREPORTS-405-150.pdf)
known_limitations: Not every useful credibility item is automatically material.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For the promise at issue in *Giglio*, the prosecutor's office was treated as the government entity, so a promise by one assistant was attributable to the government despite the trial prosecutor's lack of personal knowledge. [*Giglio*, 405 U.S. at 154](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-405/pdf/USREPORTS-405-150.pdf)
known_limitations: The holding is bounded to the prosecutor's office and the promise at issue.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The distinct *Napue* rule forbids the government from knowingly using false testimony or allowing known false testimony to go uncorrected, including falsehoods bearing on witness credibility; the materiality question asks whether there is any reasonable likelihood that the false testimony could have affected the jury's judgment. [*Napue v. Illinois*, 360 U.S. 264, 269–72 (1959)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-360/pdf/USREPORTS-360-264.pdf); [*Giglio*, 405 U.S. at 153–54](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-405/pdf/USREPORTS-405-150.pdf)
known_limitations: Knowledge, falsity, correction, and reasonable likelihood require record-specific proof.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: In a federal criminal prosecution, § 3500(a) bars subpoena, discovery, or inspection of a government or prospective government witness's statement in United States possession until that witness has testified on direct examination at trial. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(a)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Independent constitutional obligations must be classified separately.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: After a government witness testifies on direct, § 3500(b) requires the court, on the defendant's motion, to order production of a United States-possessed statement that relates to the testimony's subject matter and permits a reasonable recess for examination and preparation. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Possession, statement status, relation to testimony, and a motion must be established.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: If the government claims that part of a statement is unrelated to the testimony, § 3500(c) requires in camera inspection, excision of unrelated matter, delivery of the remainder, and preservation of withheld text for appellate review if the defendant objects. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: The statute's objection and preservation procedure must be followed.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: If the United States elects not to obey a § 3500 production order, subsection (d) requires striking the witness's testimony and continuing trial unless the court determines that the interests of justice require a mistrial. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(d)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Mistrial remains subject to the statutory interests-of-justice determination.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Section 3500(e) limits “statement” to a witness-signed or adopted writing, a substantially verbatim contemporaneous recording or transcription of the witness's oral statement, or the witness's grand-jury statement. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(e)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Notes, summaries, and reports must be tested against the statutory definition rather than labels.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 26.2(a) is reciprocal: after a nondefendant witness testifies on direct, the court must, on motion by a party who did not call the witness, order the calling side to produce a possessed statement relating to the testimony's subject matter. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 26.2(a)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The witness must have testified and the moving party must not have called the witness.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 26.2 governs production at trial, at a Rule 12 suppression hearing, and in the additional proceedings specified by Rules 5.1, 8.1, 32, 32.1, 46, and 50; disobedience requires striking the witness's testimony, with a mistrial if a government attorney disobeys and justice requires it. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 26.2(e), (g)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Proceeding-specific cross-references and sanction text must be checked.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 17(a) provides the form for a witness subpoena, and Rule 17(b) requires issuance on an indigent defendant's ex parte showing that the named witness is necessary to an adequate defense, with process costs and witness fees paid as for government witnesses. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 17(a)–(b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Necessity, service, witness fees, and any foreign service issue require the record.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Current Rule 17(c) permits a subpoena to designate documents or objects for production, permits prompt quashing or modification if compliance would be unreasonable or oppressive, and requires a court order plus ordinarily victim notice before a post-charge third-party subpoena for a victim's personal or confidential information. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 17(c)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The content, recipient, timing, victim status, and asserted burden control.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Current Rule 17(h) prohibits using Rule 17 to subpoena a witness or prospective witness's statement and directs the parties to Rule 26.2 instead. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 17(h)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Independent Rule 16, constitutional, and statutory classifications remain necessary.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For pretrial production under current Rule 17(c), *United States v. Nixon* holds that the subpoena is not a general criminal-discovery device and requires the proponent to clear relevance, admissibility, and specificity hurdles, together with the case's additional good-faith, necessity, and reasonable-availability considerations. [*United States v. Nixon*, 418 U.S. 683, 698–702 (1974)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-418/pdf/USREPORTS-418-683.pdf)
known_limitations: Circuit-specific defense applications and ex parte practice remain open.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: A substantially revised Rule 17 is projected for December 1, 2027 after the Standing Committee approved final proposed amendments in June 2026 for submission to the Judicial Conference, but it is not current law and may still be delayed, changed, rejected, or withdrawn through the rulemaking process. [U.S. Courts Rule 17 status record](https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/records-rules-committees/suggestions/new-york-city-bar-association-22-cr-a); [Pending Rules and Forms Amendments](https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/pending-rules-and-forms-amendments)
known_limitations: This verifies only current proposal status and expressly does not treat the proposal as binding law.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 12 permits a pretrial motion for a defense, objection, or request that can be decided without a trial on the merits, and Rule 47 governs the motion's form and supporting grounds. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(b)(1), 47](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: A suppression request and a Rule 14 severance request must be raised before trial when the basis is then reasonably available and the motion can be decided without a trial on the merits. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(b)(3)(C)–(D)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: At arraignment or as soon afterward as practicable, a defendant may request notice of the government's intent to use in its case-in-chief evidence discoverable under Rule 16 so the defendant has an opportunity to move to suppress; the government's voluntary notice provision is distinct. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(b)(4)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: The court may set, extend, or reset a pretrial-motion deadline; if it sets none, the deadline is the start of trial. A late Rule 12(b)(3) motion is untimely, but the court may consider it on a showing of good cause. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(c)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: The court must decide every pretrial motion before trial unless good cause supports deferral, may not defer if doing so will adversely affect a party's appeal right, and must state essential factual findings on the record. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(d)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: All suppression-hearing proceedings and oral findings and conclusions must be recorded, and Rule 26.2 applies at the hearing with a law-enforcement officer treated as a government witness. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(f), (h)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: Rule 41 distinguishes a motion to return property, filed in the seizure district with evidence received on necessary factual issues, from a defendant's suppression motion, which is filed in the trial court as Rule 12 provides. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 41(g)–(h)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: Fourth Amendment rights are personal: a defendant must show that the challenged search or seizure violated the defendant's own protected interest rather than rely solely on evidence obtained through a violation of someone else's rights. [*Rakas v. Illinois*, 439 U.S. 128, 133–40 (1978)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-439/pdf/USREPORTS-439-128.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: For privacy-based search claims, *Rakas* directs the inquiry to whether the defendant had a legitimate expectation of privacy in the place searched or thing invaded; mere presence or a target label is not enough. [*Rakas*, 439 U.S. at 140–50](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-439/pdf/USREPORTS-439-128.pdf)
known_limitations: The module's verification boundary preserves fact-specific, local, circuit-specific, and unaddressed remedial questions.
researcher_notes: Current official rules, Code text, and final Supreme Court sources reviewed through the stated date.

text: A *Franks* evidentiary hearing requires a substantial preliminary showing that a warrant-affidavit false statement was made knowingly and intentionally or with reckless disregard for truth and was necessary to probable cause; conclusory allegations or a mere desire to cross-examine do not suffice. [*Franks v. Delaware*, 438 U.S. 154, 155–56, 170–72 (1978)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-438/pdf/USREPORTS-438-154.pdf)

[28 U.S.C. §§ 2241(c), 2255(b), (e)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2255)

text: Habeas and § 2255 require qualifying custody under the challenged detention or sentence when the application or motion is filed. Custody and Article III mootness are separate inquiries and must not be collapsed into a single “jurisdiction” label. text: A transfer to another institution generally changes the physical custodian but does not by itself prove that the challenged custody injury disappeared. Respondent substitution, territorial authority, retention or transfer of the case, redressability, and any change in the challenged decision remain separate questions. [*Padilla*, 542 U.S. at 434–47](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-542/pdf/USREPORTS-542-426.pdf); [*Carafas*, 391 U.S. at 237–40](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-391/pdf/USREPORTS-391-234.pdf)

text: Later release can leave a conviction challenge live under *Carafas* while mooting a completed administrative or revocation challenge under *Spencer*. [*United States v. Cordero*, 7 F.4th 1058, 1066–68 (11th Cir. 2021)](https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/201810837.pdf)

[Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts](https://www.uscourts.gov/about-federal-courts/court-role-and-structure/about-us-district-courts)

text: Federal courts may prescribe local rules under 28 U.S.C. § 2071 and the applicable national procedural rule, and federal courts must post local rules on their public websites. [Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts](https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/current-rules-practice-procedure)

text: In the First Circuit, a federal sentence-credit request under 18 U.S.C. § 3585(b) must first be presented to the Bureau of Prisons; after administrative exhaustion, the prisoner may seek review of the BOP determination through § 2241. [*Rogers v. United States*, 180 F.3d 349, 357–58 (1st Cir. 1999)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/198520/rogers-v-united-states/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit and limited to BOP sentence-credit computation. Rogers does not supply a general catalog of exhaustion exceptions or characterize every § 2241 exhaustion rule.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Second Circuit, federal prisoners ordinarily must exhaust BOP remedies before § 2241 review; when a prisoner procedurally defaults and the administrative path has closed, review is barred unless cause and prejudice are shown. [*Carmona v. U.S. Bureau of Prisons*, 243 F.3d 629, 633–34 (2d Cir. 2001)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/772485/carlos-pelaez-edison-carmona-v-united-states-bureau-of-prisons/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit and limited to a federal disciplinary proceeding and procedural default. Legitimate circumstances beyond the prisoner's control may supply cause, but this claim does not define every excuse from ordinary exhaustion.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Third Circuit, federal prisoners ordinarily must exhaust administrative remedies before a § 2241 petition; a procedural default that closes the administrative path bars merits review unless the prisoner shows cause and prejudice. [*Moscato v. Federal Bureau of Prisons*, 98 F.3d 757, 760–62 (3d Cir. 1996)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/728093/phillip-b-moscato-08126-050-v-federal-bureau-of-prisons-lsci/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit and limited to federal institutional discipline and a defaulted administrative appeal. It does not establish that every unexhausted filing is jurisdictionally barred.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: The Fourth Circuit recognizes administrative exhaustion as a judicial restraint that can make a § 2241 petition premature, but not as a jurisdictional prerequisite to the district court's habeas power. [*Dragenice v. Ridge*, 389 F.3d 92, 98 (4th Cir. 2004)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/036717.P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fourth Circuit. Dragenice involved immigration detention and a pending removal proceeding, not the BOP Part 542 remedy program, so it does not establish BOP-specific steps or exceptions.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, a federal prisoner challenging a Parole Commission decision ordinarily must exhaust before § 2241 review; an exception requires extraordinary circumstances such as an unavailable or wholly inappropriate remedy or a patently futile course, and the prisoner bears the burden. [*Fuller v. Rich*, 11 F.3d 61, 62 (5th Cir. 1994)](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/Opinions/pub/93/93-01767.CR0.wpd.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit and limited to a Parole Commission administrative appeal. The opinion required presentation even when the appeal might be rejected as untimely and does not excuse BOP Part 542 exhaustion on speculation alone.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Sixth Circuit, federal prisoners ordinarily must exhaust before filing under § 2241, but the judge-made requirement may be excused where remedies are futile or cannot provide the relief sought, or where the administrator—not the prisoner—caused the failure; a missing final response does not automatically defeat exhaustion. [*Fazzini v. Northeast Ohio Correctional Center*, 473 F.3d 229, 231–36 (6th Cir. 2006)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/796434/paul-fazzini-v-northeast-ohio-correctional-center-warden-united-states/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Sixth Circuit and arising from a Parole Commission appeal. The opinion's treatment of what must be attached at pleading is distinct from whether a particular BOP Part 542 claim was properly exhausted.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: The Seventh Circuit applies a common-law exhaustion rule to § 2241 even though the PLRA's statutory exhaustion rule does not apply; judge-made exceptions exist, but the hurdle is high and self-created delay does not establish an excuse. [*Richmond v. Scibana*, 387 F.3d 602, 604–06 (7th Cir. 2004)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/788163/michael-richmond-v-joseph-scibana-warden-federal-correctional/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit. Richmond ultimately classified the placement-policy challenge outside § 2241, so the common-law exhaustion proposition must not be converted into a merits holding that every BOP placement challenge sounds in habeas.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, a prisoner challenging the BOP's execution of a federal sentence must first present the claim to the BOP; failure to request the available BOP designation required dismissal of the § 2241 petition without prejudice. [*Mathena v. United States*, 577 F.3d 943, 946 (8th Cir. 2009)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/09/08/082184P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit and limited to the available nunc pro tunc designation process in the sentence-execution posture. No general exception rule is inferred.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Tenth Circuit, exhaustion of available BOP remedies is a prerequisite to § 2241 relief despite the absence of an express statutory clause; a narrow futility exception exists, but alleged local categorical denial is insufficient where regional and national review remain available. [*Garza v. Davis*, 596 F.3d 1198, 1203–04 (10th Cir. 2010)](https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/01018368252.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit and limited to the BOP placement posture. A prisoner cannot establish futility merely by styling the claim as a facial regulatory challenge, but materially different facts require separate analysis.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the First Circuit, appellate review of a First Step Act § 404 ruling is deferential absent a legal benchmark error; the district court may explain its exercise of discretion briefly, and the explanation may be understood from the full record, but it must show consideration of the parties' nonfrivolous arguments. [*United States v. Rodríguez-Reyes*, No. 23-2037, slip op. at 9–15 (1st Cir. June 10, 2026)](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/sites/ca1/files/opnfiles/23-2037P-01A.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit. Rodríguez-Reyes does not require a detailed rebuttal to every argument or a sentence reduction, and the adequacy of an explanation remains record dependent.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Second Circuit, a district court is not categorically required to hold a hearing at which the defendant is present before denying a First Step Act § 404 sentence-reduction motion. [*United States v. Gadsden*, 982 F.3d 106, 112–15 (2d Cir. 2020)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca2-19-03139/pdf/USCOURTS-ca2-19-03139-0.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit and limited to the absence of a categorical hearing-and-presence requirement before denial. Gadsden does not prohibit a hearing, resolve every due-process question, or excuse compliance with Concepcion's later nationwide explanation rule.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Third Circuit, § 404 does not itself entitle a defendant to an in-person or plenary resentencing hearing, but the defendant must receive a reasonable opportunity to present written sentencing arguments, and the court must give enough explanation for meaningful appellate review. [*United States v. Shields*, 48 F.4th 183, 195–202 (3d Cir. 2022)](https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/192717p.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit. Shields does not create an entitlement to oral allocution or a plenary resentencing; its error finding turned on denying both a hearing and the requested opportunity for written sentencing submissions in the circumstances presented.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Fourth Circuit, § 404 does not require a reduction even when the existing sentence exceeds a revised statutory maximum, but the record must demonstrate that the district court considered every nonfrivolous argument presented; an ambiguous record can require vacatur and remand. [*United States v. Reed*, 58 F.4th 816, 819–23 (4th Cir. 2023)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/197368.P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fourth Circuit. Reed recognizes that Concepcion displaced Collington's mandatory-reduction rule; it does not guarantee a reduction or make every sparse order reversible.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, § 404(c)'s bar on a later motion after a prior merits denial is a mandatory claim-processing rule rather than a jurisdictional limit; when the government properly invokes the bar and the first motion received a complete merits review, the court must enforce it. [*United States v. Naranjo*, 102 F.4th 280, 283–85 (5th Cir. 2024)](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/22/22-50938-CV0.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit and limited to § 404(c)'s successive-motion bar. Naranjo does not resolve hearing rights, the merits of an initial motion, or whether a materially different prior disposition was a complete merits review.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Sixth Circuit, the § 404 benchmark recalculation incorporates only the Fair Sentencing Act's retroactive changes; the court then may consider other relevant intervening information, must reason through nonfrivolous arguments, and must explain the decision adequately for abuse-of-discretion review. [*United States v. Domenech*, 63 F.4th 1078, 1083–86 (6th Cir. 2023)](https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/23a0059p-06.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Sixth Circuit. Domenech does not require the benchmark Guidelines range to absorb nonretroactive changes and does not require a reduction; reassignment on remand was tied to the repeated failures in that record.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Seventh Circuit, the adequacy of a § 404 explanation is context dependent; a district court abuses its discretion when a materially changed record presents new nonfrivolous arguments and the ruling effectively repeats an earlier order without showing that those arguments were considered. [*United States v. Williams*, 93 F.4th 389, 391–94 (7th Cir. 2024)](https://media.ca7.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/OpinionsWeb/processWebInputExternal.pl?Path=Y2024%2FD02-20%2FC%3A23-2313%3AJ%3AWood%3Aaut%3AT%3AfnOp%3AN%3A3170766%3AS%3A0&Submit=Display)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit. Williams does not prescribe a required explanation length or guarantee relief; it addresses a current record materially different from the one underlying the earlier order.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, eligibility under § 404 is reviewed de novo and the grant or denial of an eligible motion is reviewed for abuse of discretion; the First Step Act does not require a hearing on the motion. [*United States v. McDonald*, 944 F.3d 769, 771–72 (8th Cir. 2019)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/19/12/191221P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit. McDonald's no-hearing and review holdings survive as bounded propositions; any pre-Concepcion restriction on intervening information is not adopted.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Ninth Circuit after Concepcion, a district court deciding a § 404 motion must consider the parties' nonfrivolous arguments based on intervening legal or factual developments and give a brief statement of reasons; an unexplained denial can require vacatur and remand. [*United States v. Carter*, 44 F.4th 1227, 1228–29 (9th Cir. 2022)](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/08/17/19-10411.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Ninth Circuit. Carter recognizes that Concepcion abrogated Kelley's contrary intervening-change restriction; it does not require a reduction or a detailed point-by-point opinion.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Tenth Circuit, a § 404 proceeding is a sentence modification rather than a plenary resentencing; no hearing or defendant presence is categorically required, and the discretionary disposition is reviewed for abuse of discretion with enough reasoning to permit review. [*United States v. Mannie*, 971 F.3d 1145, 1155–58 (10th Cir. 2020)](https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/010110393562.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit. Mannie's surviving nonplenary, hearing, presence, and review holdings are used; any pre-Concepcion restriction on intervening information is not adopted.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Eleventh Circuit, denial of an eligible § 404 motion is reviewed for abuse of discretion; a court may deny relief even when the existing sentence exceeds the revised statutory maximum, may not use § 404 as a collateral vehicle to invalidate the original sentence, and may satisfy Concepcion with a brief explanation evident from the record. [*United States v. Williams*, 63 F.4th 908, 912–14 (11th Cir. 2023)](https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/202112877.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eleventh Circuit. Williams does not permit a court to ignore nonfrivolous arguments, require a reduction, or decide an independent collateral attack through § 404.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the D.C. Circuit, § 404 does not create a categorical right to allocution before decision; after Concepcion, review of the discretionary ruling is not overly searching absent legal error, a sentence above the revised maximum does not itself compel reduction, and a sufficiently reasoned record can sustain denial. [*United States v. Lawrence*, 1 F.4th 40, 46–48 (D.C. Cir. 2021)](https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2021/06/20-3061-1902399.pdf); [*United States v. Smith*, 104 F.4th 314, 333–35 (D.C. Cir. 2024)](https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2024/06/22-3033-2059841.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the D.C. Circuit. Lawrence addresses no categorical allocution right, while Smith supplies the current post-Concepcion review and explanation rules; neither guarantees relief or eliminates case-specific procedural requirements.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the First Circuit, the certificate-of-appealability and appellate preclearance requirements do not directly apply to a federal prisoner's claim that actually proceeds under § 2241; whether a filing is properly classified under § 2241 rather than § 2255 remains a separate question. [*United States v. Barrett*, 178 F.3d 34, 42 (1st Cir. 1999)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/198488/united-states-v-barrett/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit and limited to the COA consequence after correct classification. Barrett involved alternative § 2255, § 2241, and All Writs Act theories; no saving-clause merits rule is adopted, and current filing-office instructions should be checked before filing.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Second Circuit, § 2253(c)'s certificate-of-appealability requirement does not apply to a federal habeas proceeding under § 2241. [*Drax v. Reno*, 338 F.3d 98, 106 n.12 (2d Cir. 2003)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/782936/drax-v-reno/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit. Drax arose from federal immigration detention; the proposition does not address state-process detention, § 2255 proceedings, or whether a filing is correctly classified under § 2241.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, a federal prisoner proceeding under § 2241 does not need a certificate of appealability to appeal the denial of the petition. [*Jeffers v. Chandler*, 253 F.3d 827, 830 (5th Cir. 2001) (per curiam)](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/Opinions/pub/99/99-41461.cv0.wpd.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit and limited to the COA rule after correct § 2241 classification. Jeffers's saving-clause merits analysis is not adopted and must be read in light of later Supreme Court law.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Sixth Circuit, no certificate of appealability is required for a § 2241 appeal when the detention arises from federal process; § 2253(c)(1)'s state-process and § 2255 categories remain controlling. [*Witham v. United States*, 355 F.3d 501, 504 (6th Cir. 2004)](https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/04a0016p-06.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Sixth Circuit. Witham involved federal court-martial process; the opinion does not eliminate a COA for state-process detention or § 2255 and does not decide whether a filing is correctly classified under § 2241.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Seventh Circuit, a federal prisoner properly proceeding under § 2241 does not need a certificate of appealability; for federal cases, § 2253(c) extends the COA requirement to § 2255 but not to § 2241. [*Walker v. O'Brien*, 216 F.3d 626, 638 (7th Cir. 2000)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/769182/jimmy-walker-v-jt-obrien-and-joseph-w-finfrock-v-craig-a-hanks/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit and limited to federal-process custody. Walker's separate treatment of state-prisoner petitions is not adopted as a nationwide rule, and proceeding classification remains a distinct inquiry.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, the certificate-of-appealability requirement does not apply to a federal prisoner effectively filing under § 2241. [*Langella v. Anderson*, 612 F.3d 938, 939 n.2 (8th Cir. 2010)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/10/07/093024P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit. Langella involved federal parole detention; no rule is adopted for state-process custody, § 2255, or disputed classification of a mislabeled filing.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Ninth Circuit, a person in federal custody does not need a certificate of appealability to appeal the denial of a properly classified § 2241 petition. [*Close v. Thomas*, 653 F.3d 970, 974 n.2 (9th Cir. 2011)](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2011/08/03/10-35850.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Ninth Circuit. Close involved federal BOP program-eligibility claims; the COA proposition does not decide § 2241 merits, state-process custody, § 2255, or filing classification.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Tenth Circuit, a federal prisoner appealing a final order in a properly classified § 2241 proceeding does not need a certificate of appealability. [*McIntosh v. U.S. Parole Commission*, 115 F.3d 809, 810 n.1 (10th Cir. 1997)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/741840/marcus-allan-mcintosh-v-united-states-parole-commission/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit. McIntosh involved federal parole revocation; the proposition does not address state-process detention, § 2255, or whether a filing is properly classified under § 2241.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Eleventh Circuit, a federal prisoner proceeding under § 2241 does not need a certificate of appealability because § 2253(c)(1)(B) reaches § 2255 proceedings, not federal-process § 2241 proceedings. [*Sawyer v. Holder*, 326 F.3d 1363, 1364 n.3 (11th Cir. 2003)](https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/200116398.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eleventh Circuit and limited to the COA question. Sawyer's saving-clause merits analysis is not adopted and must be read in light of later Supreme Court law; state-process custody and filing classification remain separate.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the D.C. Circuit, a federal prisoner proceeding under § 2241 does not need a certificate of appealability, but a person detained under D.C. Superior Court process is treated as detained pursuant to state-court process for § 2253(c)(1)(A) and does need one. [*Sugarman v. Pitzer*, 170 F.3d 1145, 1146 (D.C. Cir. 1999)](https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/1999/04/98-5522a.txt); [*Madley v. U.S. Parole Commission*, 278 F.3d 1306, 1310 (D.C. Cir. 2002)](https://openjurist.org/278/f3d/1306/madley-v-united-states-parole-commission)
known_limitations: Binding only in the D.C. Circuit. The custody-producing court controls this distinction: Sugarman addresses federal process, while Madley treats D.C. Superior Court process as state-court process for § 2253(c)(1)(A). Filing classification remains separate.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the First Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule; the court has expressly left unresolved whether, and to what extent, a defendant must present each ground to the warden before relying on it in court. [*United States v. Texeira-Nieves*, 23 F.4th 48, 52–53 (1st Cir. 2022)](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/sites/ca1/files/opnfiles/21-1034P-01A.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit. Texeira-Nieves assumed issue exhaustion rather than deciding it; this claim does not establish which factual or legal grounds must match the warden request, and it does not adopt the opinion's superseded discussion of the former policy-statement landscape.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Second Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule that the government may waive or forfeit; after the government withdrew the defense, the district court could consider the motion even if the defendant had not satisfied the prerequisite. [*United States v. Saladino*, 7 F.4th 120, 121–24 (2d Cir. 2021)](https://storage.courtlistener.com/pdf/2021/08/04/united_states_v._saladino.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit. The panel did not decide which of two competing readings of the 30-day route was correct; the separate concurrence's equitable-exception analysis is not attributed to the court.
researcher_notes: Published opinion text reviewed from the registered official source or full-text public mirror. Bounded public-source treatment review completed; comprehensive commercial citator not run; no proposition is extended outside the named circuit or posture.

text: In the Third Circuit, a defendant's § 3582(c)(1)(A) motion must be addressed first to the sentencing court; a motion made before 30 days elapsed and without completed administrative review was a roadblock that defeated first-instance appellate relief and made a limited remand futile. [*United States v. Raia*, 954 F.3d 594, 595–97 (3d Cir. 2020)](https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/201033p.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit and limited to Raia's unusual posture, where a government sentencing appeal was pending and the defendant asked the court of appeals to grant relief or remand. The claim does not rely on Raia's pandemic-specific merits observations or convert its procedural holding into a universal issue-exhaustion rule.

text: In the Fourth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s threshold requirement is nonjurisdictional and waived if not timely raised; after first asking the warden, a defendant may file upon full administrative exhaustion or 30 days after the warden's receipt, whichever occurs first, even if the warden denied the request during those 30 days. [*United States v. Muhammad*, 16 F.4th 126, 129–31 (4th Cir. 2021)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/207520.P.pdf)

text: In the Fifth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a nonjurisdictional but mandatory claim-processing rule: both statutory routes begin with a request to BOP, and a court must enforce the rule when the government properly raises it. text: In the Sixth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is nonjurisdictional but mandatory when the government timely invokes it; courts may not create a pandemic or futility exception, and a prematurely filed motion is dismissed without prejudice. [*United States v. Alam*, 960 F.3d 831, 832–36 (6th Cir. 2020)](https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/20a0171p-06.pdf)

text: In the Seventh Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is an affirmative defense and a mandatory claim-processing rule: the government can forfeit it, but the court must enforce it when the government properly invokes it. text: In the Eighth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s filing prerequisite is a mandatory claim-processing rule that must be enforced when properly raised; an unexhausted motion is dismissed without prejudice, and asserted futility based on the Attorney General's home-confinement memorandum did not excuse the missing request. [*United States v. Houck*, 2 F.4th 1082, 1084–85 (8th Cir. 2021)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/21/06/202216P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit. Houck's futility holding is limited to the theory actually presented; compassionate release and BOP home-confinement placement remain distinct remedies.

text: In the Ninth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a mandatory claim-processing rule enforced when the government invokes it; a renewed motion based on changed circumstances required a new qualifying BOP request, and the filing defect was not cured by the passage of 30 days while the motion was pending. [*United States v. Keller*, 2 F.4th 1278, 1281–84 (9th Cir. 2021)](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2021/07/01/20-50247.pdf)

text: In the Tenth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule that the government can waive or forfeit; when the government abandoned its exhaustion argument on appeal, the court proceeded to the merits. text: In the D.C. Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule; the court expressly declined to decide whether each ground later presented in court must first have been presented to the warden. [*United States v. Wilson*, 77 F.4th 837, 842–45 (D.C. Cir. 2023)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-caDC-21-03074/pdf/USCOURTS-caDC-21-03074-0.pdf)

text: In the First Circuit, a pending appeal from a supervised-release revocation does not divest the district court of its continuing § 3583(e)(2) authority to modify release conditions during the term of supervision. [*United States v. D'Amario*, 412 F.3d 253, 255–56 (1st Cir. 2005)](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/sites/ca1/files/opnfiles/04-2566-01A.pdf)

text: In the Second Circuit, a court deciding whether to modify or terminate supervised release must consider the § 3583(e) subset of § 3553(a) factors, but it need not make a separate factual finding on each factor; a statement, read with the record, that the statutory factors were considered is sufficient. [*United States v. Gammarano*, 321 F.3d 311, 315–16 (2d Cir. 2003)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/781046/united-states-v-john-gammarano/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit. Gammarano does not require a particular explanation length, create a presumption of termination, or decide whether changed circumstances are required for condition modification; Parisi separately clarifies that they are not.

text: In the Third Circuit, § 3583(e)(1) does not require an exceptional, extraordinary, new, or unforeseen circumstance before early termination may be granted, although changed circumstances may often be relevant to the discretionary assessment. text: In the Fourth Circuit, § 3583(e)(1) ordinarily authorizes a conduct-based inquiry and permits consideration of a broad range of interests-of-justice factors, but it is not a mechanism for collaterally attacking an original, unappealed sentence. [*United States v. Pregent*, 190 F.3d 279, 282–83 (4th Cir. 1999)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/Published/986309.P.pdf)

text: In the Fifth Circuit, changed circumstances are not a jurisdictional prerequisite to modifying a supervised-release condition under § 3583(e)(2), but illegality alone is not one of the enumerated grounds and cannot itself supply the basis for modification. text: In the Sixth Circuit, § 3583(e)(1) does not make exceptionally good behavior an absolute prerequisite to early termination; conduct and changed circumstances remain relevant within the statute's broader discretionary inquiry. text: In the Seventh Circuit, an early-termination ruling must give some indication that the district court considered the statutory factors; a blanket policy of waiting until only twelve months of supervision remain circumvents § 3583(e)(1)'s individualized process. [*United States v. Lowe*, 632 F.3d 996, 998–99 (7th Cir. 2011)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca7-10-02832/pdf/USCOURTS-ca7-10-02832-0.pdf)

text: In the Eighth Circuit, Rule 32.1(c)(1) does not require counsel or a hearing before a court denies a motion to terminate supervision or modify conditions, and § 3583(e) does not require a separate explanation for denial when the existing record makes the court's basis discernible. text: In the First Circuit, assuming audita querela survives in federal criminal cases, it can address only a legal objection arising after conviction that is not redressable through another postconviction remedy; equitable hardship alone is insufficient. [*United States v. Holder*, 936 F.2d 1, 2–5 (1st Cir. 1991)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/563216/united-states-v-ewart-mark-holder/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit. Holder expressly did not decide whether audita querela survives; it rejected a pure-equity immigration-consequence theory and did not identify any actual remedial gap. Section 2255 classification and the current nationwide limits, including Jones v. Hendrix, still must be applied independently.

text: In the Second Circuit, audita querela supplies at most a hypothetical avenue when the complete absence of collateral review would raise serious constitutional questions; a nonretroactive Booker claim did not create that circumstance or a remedial gap. known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit. Richter did not hold that the writ lies in any actual case, did not make statutory nonretroactivity a constitutional defect, and predates Jones v. Hendrix; no post-Jones expansion or exception is inferred.

text: In the Third Circuit, the All Writs Act is residual and cannot displace § 2255: a federal-sentence claim cognizable under § 2255 cannot be recast as audita querela, and prior use of § 2255 or the successive-motion gate does not create a gap. known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit. Massey involved a Booker sentencing claim by a prisoner who had already pursued § 2255; it does not establish that audita querela survives or define relief outside § 2255's field.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, assuming audita querela survives in criminal cases, it is limited to a postjudgment legal objection unavailable through another postconviction remedy; purely equitable grounds are insufficient. text: In the Seventh Circuit, audita querela would require a legal defense or discharge arising after judgment; equity, harsh collateral consequences, or gross injustice alone does not satisfy that requirement. [*United States v. Johnson*, 962 F.2d 579, 581–83 (7th Cir. 1992)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/582608/united-states-v-manapurath-eappen-johnson/)

text: In the Tenth Circuit, a federal prisoner cannot use audita querela to challenge a conviction or sentence when the claim is cognizable under § 2255; the substance of the filing controls and a custody-based collateral attack may be treated as a § 2255 motion subject to the applicable authorization rules. [*United States v. Torres*, 282 F.3d 1241, 1245–46 & n.6 (10th Cir. 2002)](https://storage.courtlistener.com/pdf/2002/02/21/United_States_vs._Torres.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit. Torres assumed without deciding that audita querela might survive, distinguished coram nobis by custody, and tied notice before recharacterization to whether the filing would be the prisoner's first § 2255 motion.

text: In the Eleventh Circuit, audita querela may not be granted when the challenge is cognizable under § 2255; after recharacterization, an unauthorized second or successive motion remains outside the district court's jurisdiction. [*United States v. Holt*, 417 F.3d 1172, 1174–75 (11th Cir. 2005) (per curiam)](https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/200415848.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eleventh Circuit. Holt did not hold that audita querela survives for claims outside § 2255; it addressed a constitutional sentencing attack by a prisoner with a prior § 2255 motion and an absent successive-motion authorization.

text: In the D.C. Circuit, audita querela cannot rest on pure equity and, if it survives at all, can reach only a legal objection not cognizable through existing federal postconviction remedies; a claim cognizable under § 2255 belongs there.
